title: Chapter XLVI

teacherSummary.text: Letters from Jane report that Lydia has run off with Wickham, possibly not married. Darcy finds Elizabeth distraught; she confides in him. Elizabeth and the Gardiners hurry home.

vocabulary.context: Her affections had been continually fluctuating, but never without an object.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “fluctuate”: luc (Latin lux, "light") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To put into action or motion
vocabulary.context: Elizabeth, though expecting no less, thanked him with tears of gratitude; and all three being actuated by one spirit, everything relating to their journey was speedily settled.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “actuate”: ac- (Latin ad, "to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To come, or be placed, in the room of
vocabulary.context: Her pale face and impetuous manner made him start, and before he could recover himself enough to speak, she, in whose mind every idea was superseded by Lydia’s situation, hastily exclaimed, “I beg your pardon, but I must leave you.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “supersede”: super- (Latin super, "above"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Lydia left a few lines for his wife, informing her of their intention.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “inform”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + form (Latin forma, "shape"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.etymology: “dart”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: The act of seizing or taking hold of
vocabulary.context: With the kindest concern he came on to Longbourn, and broke his apprehensions to us in a manner most creditable to his heart.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: Without allowing herself time for consideration, and scarcely knowing what she felt, Elizabeth on finishing this letter instantly seized the other, and opening it with the utmost impatience, read as follows: it had been written a day later than the conclusion of the first.

vocabulary.etymology: “finishing”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The state or quality of being hidden
vocabulary.context: He readily assured her of his secrecy—again expressed his sorrow for her distress, wished it a happier conclusion than there was at present reason to hope, and leaving his compliments for her relations, with only one serious, parting, look, went away.

vocabulary.etymology: “secrecy”: se- (Latin se-, "apart"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To make trial or experiment of

vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “attempt”: at- (Latin ad, "to") + tempt (Latin temptare, "to try"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: An unmarried elopement could ruin the reputation of an entire family.

significance: The crisis tests Darcy's love and reveals Elizabeth's change of heart.
discussionQuestions: Why does Elizabeth tell Darcy, and what does she fear?
Where does plot appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with first impressions and prejudice?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XLVI,” how does Austen show scandal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XLVI develops the idea of scandal. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and conflict shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses plot in Chapter XLVI to complicate the reader's understanding of scandal. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XLVI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of scandal responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XLVI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of scandal. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.passage: Without allowing herself time for consideration, and scarcely knowing what she felt, Elizabeth on finishing this letter instantly seized the other, and opening it with the utmost impatience, read as follows: it had been written a day later than the conclusion of the first.

annotationFocus.label: Conflict

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why does Elizabeth tell Darcy, and what does she fear? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are fluctuating, actuated, superseded, informing, darting. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Her affections had been continually fluctuating, but never without an object.” Webster's says: To move as a wave. Now the word history: “fluctuate”: luc (Latin lux, "light") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “actuate”: ac- (Latin ad, "to"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “supersede”: super- (Latin super, "above"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. An unmarried elopement could ruin the reputation of an entire family. Why does this chapter matter? The crisis tests Darcy's love and reveals Elizabeth's change of heart. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for plot.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see plot, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to scandal.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Plot, Conflict, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of plot. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Plot, Conflict, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XLVI,” how does Austen show scandal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about scandal, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how plot shapes scandal. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
